failures.text: How does an idea get from a draft all the way to paper trading with real allocated capital?
failures.answer: Sir, an idea climbs a fixed staircase: a draft appears only when a counted pattern fires (for example the same missed situation on 3 of 7 sessions), then your yes registers it, so the study is written down before it runs. It is tested on 2000-2023 only, against a the strict pass mark for every version tried, then runs as a paper shadow book for 20 recorded sessions. It is admitted only if it beats random picks and the average stock on 10 separate sessions after costs, a check that no future data leaked in passes, and you say yes; only then may the allocated paper capital use it, and the final real-money gate comes after that. Today nothing has been admitted: the stock rules are 6 to 8 of 20 shadow sessions in and the options line is 5 of 20.

problems.why: It leans on unexplained insider terms such as 'fixed staircase', 'paper shadow book', 'registers it' and 'no future data leaked', which a beginner would not follow, and the dense stages are hard to read.

results.text: Explain the versions tested: what a version is, how many held up and on what data, which ones matter for my money, and what was rejected.
results.answer: Sir, a version is one exact setting of an idea, such as RSI over 70 against a different cut-off, or a 7% stop against a 10% one. Ananta has tested 1,387 of them across 168 studies, trained on 2000-2017 and checked on 2018-2023 at a the strict pass mark, with 2024 onward kept sealed. Only 70 held up (33 fully, 37 with conditions), while 487 were rejected, 155 showed the reverse of the claim, and 650 had too little data to say. For your money the ones that matter are filters on what to avoid: don't buy more than 20% above the 50-day average or with RSI over 70, and a fixed stop beat a trailing one. Moving-average crossovers, MACD crosses, candlestick patterns and the expiry-eve strangle were rejected, so none is a usable signal.

results.text: What happens if Ajanta Pharma opens 3% up on Monday morning?
results.answer: Sir, the managed book would skip the buy. Its rule is that a buy opening more than 2% above the last close is skipped, and 2% above Friday's Rs 3,509 is about Rs 3,579, so a 3% gap-up open near Rs 3,614 is over the line. The roughly Rs 12,200 meant for it would stay in cash, and the plan doesn't say it chases the stock later. The JIOFIN sale is a separate cut in the plan, so the gap doesn't touch it. This is all on paper; nothing is placed from chat.

results.text: Has any stock rule of yours actually proved itself yet? Be honest.
results.answer: No, sir: no stock rule has proved itself yet. The stock rules are 9 of 20 practice sessions of the 20 needed in, and Ananta has beaten chance and the average stock on 5 of the 10 days it needs. What has held up in testing are filters on what to avoid, such as not chasing a stock far above its 50-day average, and those are not buy signals. Until the 20-session trial is finished, treat the stock picks as practice only.

results.text: Walk me through what you do every day, start to finish, in order.
results.answer: Sir, each evening after the 3:30 pm close Ananta takes in the day's prices, flows and your Zerodha snapshot, re-rates every holding and writes the cut list. Then the managed book fills yesterday's plan at the open, checks its 7% stops and writes tomorrow's plan, and the practice book records the next session's practice picks and the daily call. At night the reconstruction replays the day like a coach, covering what it held, what it missed and what to look into. At 8:30 am Indian time the morning view comes out, and between 9:15 and 10:15 the options line decides on one index lot; everything is paper and nothing is placed from chat.

results.text: Tata Power is up 24% for me. Why trim a winner?
results.answer: Sir, Ananta isn't trimming it because it is a winner; the trim is about size and strength. Tata Power is 25% of your stocks (about Rs 26,900), and Ananta rates it only 46/100, middling, with the price 3.5% under its 50-day and 9.8% under its 200-day average. A +24% gain doesn't make a middling stock safer: it is down 8% over 3 months and 26% below its 52-week high. Its suggestion is to bring it toward 15% (about Rs 10,600 of it), which on paper locks in part of the gain and cuts how much one stock can hurt you; it would be wrong if the price climbs back above Rs 347, its one-month average.

results.text: What exactly is your job for me? One paragraph.
results.answer: Sir, my job is to be your assistant for the Indian market, on paper only: nothing is placed from chat. Each evening I re-rate every holding in your account and write a cut list, and I keep a paper copy of your account that moves money between stocks, options and cash inside set limits. A separate paper book acts on that cut list and buys replacements from the Nifty 500 by filters that have been tested. I also write the morning view, run Ananta's research and tests, and answer your questions honestly, including when a call is wrong or an idea has not been tested.

results.text: If RSI is 28 on the Nifty daily, what does that tell you, and what would you do?
results.answer: Sir, an RSI of 28 (a 0-100 gauge where under 30 means oversold) says the Nifty has been sold hard and a bounce is more likely than usual, but it does not say the fall is over. Ananta tested this on stocks: those bought at RSI under 30 earned about 2% more over the next 20 sessions than other days, in both 2000-2017 and 2018-2023. It hasn't tested RSI under 30 on the Nifty index itself, so that evidence is moderate and only for stocks. The nearest paper rule is the stock reversal rule, which buys oversold stocks and has no rule for the index. For the index I would treat 28 as a reason to look, not to buy in one go; if you hold or start an index fund, small staggered amounts suit it better. For reference, the Nifty's RSI is 54 on the 30 Oct close, so this isn't the case today.

results.text: What is the one risk rule that stops a bad day from becoming a bad month?
results.answer: Sir, it is the rule that stops trading for the day after a 5% loss: when realised plus open loss reaches 5% of the equity at the start of the session, every position is closed and there are no new entries that day. It works during market hours only, so an overnight gap can still take a bigger loss than 5%. The month-level backstop is the rule that pauses trading after a 22% fall below the account's peak, which stops new buys until you resume. For now that one is only logged on paper, by your decision of 19 Oct, and the books keep trading.

The managed book acts on the cut list and buys a replacement for each cut, and it has not traded yet: session 1 of 60 is Monday 2 Nov, when its first plan runs. Both are judged at 60 sessions against your holdings left as they were, and nothing is read into either before then.
